title: UPDATE
summary: Change existing rows: one, some, or computed from other tables.

steps.title: UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE
body: - `SET` can change several columns at once, separated by commas.
- The right-hand side can be any expression, including the column itself: `SET km = km + 15`.
- **WHERE decides which rows change.** Leave it out and *every row* changes. There is no undo button outside a transaction (lesson 4).
> **Habit:** write the `SELECT ... WHERE` first, check it returns exactly the rows you mean, then turn it into the UPDATE with the same WHERE.

steps.title: Into the workshop
prompt: Bike **B15** has been towed to the depot: set its **status** to `repair` and its **station** to NULL.
Tables:
- `stations(name, district, docks)`
- `bikes(id, model, station, status, km)`: `status` defaults to `'ok'` and `km` to `0`; `station` is NULL for a bike in the depot
- `repairs(id, bike_id, reported, issue, fixed)`: `id` is assigned automatically; `fixed` defaults to `0`
- `incoming(id, model)`: new bikes delivered to the depot

steps.title: Updating from other tables
body: Often the new value lives in **another table**. A correlated subquery works everywhere:
WHERE id IN (SELECT bike_id FROM repairs WHERE fixed = 1);
SET docks = docks + (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM incoming)
Joined updates are spelled differently per database:
FROM bikes AS b JOIN repairs AS r ON r.bike_id = b.id
UPDATE bikes AS b JOIN repairs AS r ON r.bike_id = b.id

steps.prompt: Will the statement change every row of `bikes`?
items: `UPDATE bikes SET status = 'ok' WHERE station IS NULL;`
`UPDATE bikes SET km = 0 WHERE id IN (SELECT bike_id FROM repairs);`
steps.explain: `WHERE 1 = 1` is true for every row. `SET km = km` 'changes' every row to its own value; the database still writes them.

steps.title: Close the open repairs
prompt: The workshop finished every repair on bikes currently in `repair` status. Set **fixed = 1** for every **unfixed** repair whose bike has status `repair`.
Tables:
- `stations(name, district, docks)`
- `bikes(id, model, station, status, km)`: `status` defaults to `'ok'` and `km` to `0`; `station` is NULL for a bike in the depot
- `repairs(id, bike_id, reported, issue, fixed)`: `id` is assigned automatically; `fixed` defaults to `0`
- `incoming(id, model)`: new bikes delivered to the depot
solution: AND bike_id IN (SELECT id FROM bikes WHERE status = 'repair');

steps.title: Back on the street
prompt: Every bike with status `repair` whose repairs are **all fixed** (no row in `repairs` with `fixed = 0`) can return to service. Set those bikes' **status** to `ok` and **station** to `Harbour Gate`.
In this copy of the data, B21's flat tyre has been fixed, but B44's cracked frame hasn't.
Tables:
- `stations(name, district, docks)`
- `bikes(id, model, station, status, km)`: `status` defaults to `'ok'` and `km` to `0`; `station` is NULL for a bike in the depot
- `repairs(id, bike_id, reported, issue, fixed)`: `id` is assigned automatically; `fixed` defaults to `0`
- `incoming(id, model)`: new bikes delivered to the depot
solution: AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM repairs AS r WHERE r.bike_id = bikes.id AND r.fixed = 0);
